beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Here is a corner of the multiplication table. Its numbers make patterns, and every pattern has a reason.

do.label: What belongs in the empty cell?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Know the reason, and the table can fill in its own missing squares. One is missing right here.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Maybe sixty-three goes in the empty square?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Make the table tell us. A row goes across.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A column goes down.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Each cell holds its row number times its column number. That answer is called a product.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: The neighbors are clues. But why do the numbers change?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: An array has equal rows. Here are seven rows of eight: fifty-six squares.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Slide in one more row. Eight squares arrive together.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Eight rows of eight. Sixty-four! The row number went up one, but the total went up eight.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: How many squares were added, from seven rows to eight rows?

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Eight. We're counting the new row.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Another row of eight. Nine rows, seventy-two.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: One step down this column adds one whole row of eight. That's why the step is eight.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Cover the missing product again. Start at seventy-two.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Slide the last row away. Eight fewer leaves sixty-four.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Sixty-four! And removing another row brings us back to fifty-six.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Add eight. Both neighbors lead to sixty-four.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: That was a step down a column. Now take a step across a row. Three times five is fifteen. What changes when five becomes six?

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: One more square in each of three rows. Add three: eighteen.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Another step adds three again. Twenty-one.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Three rows, so every step across adds three.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Here is a different kind of pattern. Four times a number always comes out even. Why? Start with four rows of seven. Split them into two rows and two rows.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Fourteen in each half. Double fourteen is twenty-eight: two equal groups of whole squares, so twenty-eight is even.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Doubling means adding a number to itself. Every square has a partner in the other half.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Is that only true for seven? Try two more.

do.text: Why is the total always even?

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Four rows of three: six and six, twelve.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Four rows of five: ten and ten, twenty.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Any whole number in each row works. Four rows always split into two rows and two rows. Two equal halves.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A table can also come from a story. This one pairs boxes with pencils. Every box holds the same amount. Two boxes hold eight pencils. How many in one box?

do.text: How many pencils in one box?

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Eight divided by two is four pencils per box.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: One more box adds four: three boxes hold twelve.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Five boxes hold twenty. The table skips four boxes, so I add two boxes: eight extra pencils.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: For twenty pencils, I work backward. Divide by four pencils per box: five boxes.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Here is another story. Ava is eight years older than Finn. When Finn is three, Ava is eleven. Each section of the bar is one year. Here the rule adds eight.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: When Finn is five, Ava is thirteen. Both grow, but the eight extra years stay the same.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: To find Finn when Ava is eighteen, subtract eight. Ten. The story decides whether we add or multiply.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: One more pattern in the table. Twelve shows up twice: at three times four, and at four times three.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Three rows of four turn into four rows of three. Same twelve squares: matching products across the diagonal.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Some patterns repeat instead of grow. Which two shapes fill the empty places?

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Circle, triangle, square. That is the shortest repeating part.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: It fits again, in the same order.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Start the part again: circle, then triangle. Square finishes it. The whole pattern keeps the same order.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A step across the row: one more in each group.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: An even column: split into two equal halves.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Matching products across the diagonal: same array, turned around.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: I can predict the next number because I know what changed.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A pattern in the table is an array telling you something. Ask it why.
